newsitem.title: GUINEA: Ousted Sierra Leone president prepares for comeback.
newsitem.headline: Ousted Sierra Leone president prepares for comeback.

text.p: Sierra Leone's president, Ahmad Tejan Kabbah, overthrown in a coup on May 25, said on Friday he was optimistic that his party faithful and foreign friends would help restore him as head of state in Freetown.

"We are here working out strategies to get things working again in Sierra Leone -- for example how to reconstruct records for the Finance Ministry and central bank which were both destroyed," said Kabbah, who is in Conakry with former finance minister Thaimu Bangura and his economic adviser Jim Funna.
"The people who claim to be in charge now don't have the slightest clue how to run a government."

Kabbah told Reuters arrangements for his return were in the hands of the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS), which is expected to hold a summit next week in the Nigerian capital Abuja to discuss Sierra Leone.
He said he expected to be back in Freetown "pretty soon".
"I know the people of Sierra Leone are solidly behind me...although we clearly need external help to restore and moreover maintain law and order," he said.

Kabbah said he was pessimistic about the prospects for a negotiated solution, not least because rebels of the Revolutionary United Front (RUF) allied to the coup leaders appeared to be calling the shots in Freetown.

"The coup really was a miscalculation on the part of the soldiers," Kabbah said. "They thought that bringing in the RUF would bring control and they would become chummy, but they were naive in that respect. Instead the RUF has unleashed a terror that went completely out of control."

Nigeria has built up its forces in Freetown since Monday's unsuccessful show of force which turned into a rout when RUF rebels turned on Nigerian forces defending foreigners at a hotel. A truce has held since then, but Kabbah said the Nigerians could strike again.
"I'm getting clear messages from my people in Freetown that they want the Nigerians to do whatever is necessary to drive these men out," Kabbah said.

"People are traumatised and have come to the end of their wits. Every night is one of terror. I believe people are willing to endure military action by ECOWAS if that's ultimately the only way to get rid of these men."
Kabbah was elected in March 1996 after four years of army rule.

He rejected accusations that his Sierra Leone People's Party government had hastened its own downfall by ignoring signs of growing discontent within the military and fuelling ethnic tensions by marginalising the national army in favour of the civilian militia of Kamajor hunters.

"We inherited a situation where the army was receiving one third of the national budget, which is excessive by any means," he said. "At the same time, we knew we had inherited a very fragile security situation, so we were very conscious of trying to balance the two."
He said the Kamajors, dominated by members of his own Mende tribe, were making a valuable contribution to maintenance of law and order in their districts.
He welcomed the leading role played by Nigeria, the current ECOWAS president, and said that comments on the irony of a military-ruled country defending the civilian government in another were unfair.
"Nigeria's position on Sierra Leone should be commended by the international community, and it should give the indication that Nigeria is moving in the right direction," he said.
